top_articles.summary: Release: llm-gemini 0.35 I added support to llm-gemini for the new Gemini 4 Argon model, made available today via the Gemini API and for customers of their $100/month subscription plan. Here are the low, medium and high pelicans . As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their staff have invested in SVG specifically (and who have boasted about their pelicans before.) Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents: The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra. But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5. Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness. One useful clue for that comes from Artificial Analysis, who publish the total cost to run their benchmark using each model. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models. top_articles.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
top_articles.title_original: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
top_articles.summary: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied : Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do. As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that: Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. top_articles.title: LaTeX renderer
top_articles.title_original: LaTeX renderer
top_articles.summary: Tool: LaTeX renderer Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app Tiny Little Office , which provides a suite of web app content editors (a Word Processor, Outliner, Presentation Builder, Spreadsheet, Calculator, Drawing Tool, Diagram Maker, Animator, Calendar, and Trip Planner). Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the #fragment section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link. It also has an llms.txt file telling agents how to construct URLs that will render as documents. Claude used that file to generate this link to a deck that explains how the URL format works: Tiny Little Office inspired me to have Claude Code (Opus 5.5 Extra) build a similar tool that works with LaTeX. Here's the sequence of prompts I used: I want a tool where you can link to it with a fragment hash #code-here and it treats that code as LaTeX and renders it really effectively. It should also support a prefix which means the latex is compressed with a custom compression dictionary optimized for latex. Use the best available latex render library from a CDN (consider WebAssembly too). If loaded without a fragment hash show an editor you can paste latex into and then toggle to a "rendered" view. That rendered view should be bookmarkable. The #fragment view should let you switch to edit source too. Since it was working in my tools repo I told it to take inspiration from the <iframe sandbox="..."> mechanism used by my existing SVG in Markdown tool as protection against XSS risks: Safe from XSS? We could run in an iframe sandbox like we do on the SVG markdown render project I had it copy the Gist/URL loading feature from that tool as well: We should have an option to load latex from a URL (or gist) similar to the markdown SVG tool Here's an example link . The tool uses Pako 2.1.0 , MathJax 4.1.3 , faster-latex 0.3.1 , and DOMPurify 3.4.16 . Tags: latex , paul-ford , tools , urls , ai , generative-ai , llms

top_articles.title: 中国信通院：6 月国内词元日均消耗量约 500 万亿，是 2025 年 12 月的近 4 倍
top_articles.title_original: 中国信通院：6 月国内词元日均消耗量约 500 万亿，是 2025 年 12 月的近 4 倍
top_articles.summary: IT之家 10 月 24 日消息，据中国信通院，随着大模型技术的迅速迭代，词元（Token）服务成为从技术走向应用的关键点，我国日均词元调用量持续攀升，2026 年 6 月， 国内词元日均消耗量约 500 万亿 ，是 2025 年 12 月的近 4 倍。产业中越来越多的 MaaS（Model as a Service，模型即服务）平台厂商通过公有云 API 方式供给大模型词元服务。然而用户对词元服务性能缺乏直观的判断依据，且面临选型困难等各类问题。 为有效衡量服务性能，中国信息通信研究院（简称“中国信通院”）人工智能研究所、人工智能大模型及软硬件评测工业和信息化部重点实验室和中国人工智能产业发展联盟，自 2025 年以来持续开展公有云大模型词元服务性能监测工作，为产业应用提供重要参考，现联合发布《大模型词元服务性能监测报告（2026 年）》。 报告基于 2026 年 1-8 月的监测数据，围绕各平台词元服务调用成功率、吞吐速度、首词时延、稳定性、价格、上下文窗口等维度开展分析，对比原厂大模型官方平台，以及 DeepSeek、Qwen、GLM、Kimi 四款开源模型在第三方平台上的性能差异，进一步分析影响词元服务性能的关键因素，总结产业核心观察，明确下一步工作计划，旨在为用户选型提供参考，并为产业界优化服务能力提供方向指引。 IT之家附报告核心观点： 1. 国内词元服务每秒吞吐量较 2025 年翻倍，仍低于国外 报告提出，8 月份国内各模型平均 TPS（每秒输出词元数）达到 78.23（个 / 秒），与 2025 年均值 38.25（个 / 秒）相比实现翻倍。但 8 月份国外典型模型的 TPS 均值为 112.82（个 / 秒），与 2025 年 12 月的 51.35（个 / 秒）相比，提升亦超过一倍，整体优于国内。 ▲ 所有大模型词元服务月均 TPS 2. 词元服务时延有所增加，国内外趋势一致 报告提出，今年以来，国内各模型的平均 TTFT（首词时延）呈现持续提升态势，8 月份均值达到 1.26 秒，相较于 2025 年平均值 0.78 秒明显增加。但同时 8 月份国外典型模型 TTFT 平均值达到 2.08 秒，相比 4 月份 1.04 秒亦明显增加。值得注意的是，TTFT 上升并非单纯的性能退化，而是伴随着模型参数量增加、上下文长度增加、调用量增加等多种因素同步产生的结果。 ▲ 所有大模型词元服务的月均 TTFT 3. 2026 年词元服务价格明显回升 报告提出，经历了过去两年价格战后，2026 年国内外模型服务价格明显上涨。国内 2025 下半年归一化均价为 6.8 元，而今年以来均价为 13.46 元，涨幅接近 1 倍。但国外价格仍高于国内，2026 年以来发布的典型模型平均归一价格约为 117.8 元。 ▲ 国内原厂大模型发布时归一化价格趋势图 4. 模型上下文长度不断向百万级长度扩展 报告提出，被监测的模型中，上下文长度达到 1M（1 百万词元）的模型占比 47.8%，200K 及以上的合计达 95.7%，相比 2025 年底的占比提高超过 76 个百分点，而低于 200K 的模型占比持续减少。 ▲ 国内原厂大模型发布时归一化价格趋势图 5. 开源模型词元服务性能提升显著，同一模型在不同平台性能波动较大 报告提出，5 月份更新了 4 款开源模型的新版本进行监测，结果显示 TPS 持续提升，TTFT 时延不断压缩。例如 8 月份 DeepSeek-V4-Pro 的 TPS 已达到 DeepSeek-V3.2 的 2 倍。时延方面，5 月份主要模型完成换代升级后，TTFT 普遍出现阶段性上升，随着推理优化措施落地，时延指标逐步回落至换代前水平。同时，4 款模型在不同平台上的 TPS、TTFT、调用成功率表现不一。部分第三方平台性能明显优于官方平台提供的模型服务，同一模型在不同平台间的 TPS 差距最大可接近一倍。各平台对相同模型的推理加速、优化策略、成本控制不同，是造成性能分化的主要原因。 ▲ 开源模型性能综合对比图

top_articles.title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?
top_articles.title_original: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.28763v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (https://github.com/maszhongming/agent4sci) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MingZhong/agent4sci).

top_articles.title: StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and Training Autonomous Operator Agents
top_articles.title_original: StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and Training Autonomous Operator Agents
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.10942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning environments are now a primary lever for improving large language model (LLM) capabilities in post-training, yet most agentic benchmarks remain static: the world moves only when the agent acts, the reward is a terminal verdict, and the pass bar is set arbitrarily. We introduce StoreBench, a live-commerce environment in which an agent runs a mid-size online apparel store on a production-grade commerce backend, testing long-horizon planning and economic judgment under uncertainty. Customers order around the clock, suppliers reprice and fail, and market shocks arrive with partial or no warning. The agent acts through the same 29 merchant tools a human operator would use, under a windowed operation budget that makes simulated time a function of actions taken, so model latency cannot influence simulated time. Pass thresholds are calibrated against scripted anchor policies, the reward is hardened against a catalogue of reward hacks, and every episode replays identically given a sequence of actions. We evaluate seven frontier LLMs on 11 scenarios of 30 to 45 days and a full simulated year, over three world seeds at matched reasoning effort. No model matches the scripted smart-triage policy on average: the best, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, passes 49% of task-seed cells against the heuristic's 97%. Human experts working through the same tools and budgets outscore every model (mean composite 0.708 vs. 0.700). Over a full simulated year under the Claude Code harness, most models show dramatic performance improvement. In a GRPO post-training run, Qwen3.5-27B trained on only five disjoint tasks raises its mean composite on the held-out evaluation tasks from 0.136 to 0.373. We release five example training-split tasks, ten sample trajectories, and the scoring and verification tooling; the full environment and evaluation suite are withheld to keep the benchmark uncontaminated.

top_articles.title: Behavior Beyond Text: Evaluating Refusal Transfer Failure in LLM Agents
top_articles.title_original: Behavior Beyond Text: Evaluating Refusal Transfer Failure in LLM Agents
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.28982v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While large language models are increasingly deployed as tool-calling agents, their safety evaluations still focus primarily on their ability to refuse harmful requests in text. We investigate whether the refusal behavior in text transfers to tool use. We construct a benchmark of 2,304 prompts across four domains, consisting of matched triplets that present the same harmful or benign request in text-only, standard tool-enabled, and adversarially framed tool-enabled settings. We then assess tool-call safety using 20 predefined forbidden actions. Testing five models of varying sizes and families, we find that requests refused in text frequently result in unsafe tool calls. Under standard tool-enabled prompting, this divergence occurs for 10-52 percent of harmful requests refused in chat. To mechanistically investigate this gap, we identify a refusal-associated direction in the residual stream of each of the five models. We find that in tool-enabled contexts, the activations along this direction decrease in four of five models. Furthermore, lower activation predicts unsafe tool calls across all five models (AUC 0.76-0.86). However, restoring the signal to the respective text-only value through activation patching only prevents a subset of unsafe calls, primarily by suppressing tool use rather than by producing safer calls. Steering along the refusal direction nearly eliminates unsafe calls only at strengths that also suppress benign tool use or degrade the output quality. Our findings indicate that the identified refusal direction contributes to whether a model acts, but only partially explains the refusal divergence. Therefore, evaluating the safety of tool-calling agents requires directly examining their actions along with their textual responses.

top_articles.title: Spectral Smoothing and Spiking Perturbations Reconfigure Capability Profiles and Selective Task Performance in Large Language Models
top_articles.title_original: Spectral Smoothing and Spiking Perturbations Reconfigure Capability Profiles and Selective Task Performance in Large Language Models
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.30676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Singular-value spectra encode important structure in transformer feed-forward projections, yet their causal role in downstream behavior remains underexplored. We study post-hoc spectral smoothing and spiking interventions on the up_proj and down_proj matrices. Positive perturbation stretches deviations from the geometric mean, making large singular values larger and small ones smaller (spiking), and vice versa. The intervention preserves singular vectors and the geometric mean of the singular values. Across five open Llama and Qwen instruction models, we evaluate the perturbed systems on capability-labeled subtasks, standard and chain-of-thought reasoning benchmarks, judge-scored truthfulness, hallucination, and safety tasks, and TRAIT personality probes. To interpret score shifts, we fit responses in a three-dimensional capability basis consisting of factual knowledge, language understanding, and deductive reasoning. The induced changes suggest structured rather than purely random sensitivity: large positive perturbations more reliably suppress language and deductive responses, moderate negative perturbations can sometimes improve factual or task-local performance on the evaluated grids, and sensitivity varies strongly by model family, benchmark module, and underlying layerwise spectral inequality. These results position spectral perturbation as a lightweight intervention for probing how capabilities are organized and traded off in large language models.

top_articles.title: IFC-MCQ: Automatically Generating Multiple-Choice Benchmarks for Evaluating LLM Agents on IFC Data Retrieval
top_articles.title_original: IFC-MCQ: Automatically Generating Multiple-Choice Benchmarks for Evaluating LLM Agents on IFC Data Retrieval
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.30533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Industry Foundation Classes (IFC), the standard for building information exchange in architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC), is increasingly queried through large language models (LLMs) using natural language. Evaluating these systems at scale is difficult because free-text answers require costly human or LLM-based review. We propose IFC-MCQ, a method that automatically generates multiple-choice benchmarks from IFC files for exact option-set grading. The taxonomy covers 15 categories and 36 subtypes across four groups, with answer keys derived from the file and distractors constructed from file-derived values or predefined rules. We applied IFC-MCQ to IFC models of varying sizes and modelling characteristics to assess generation coverage and evaluated two agentic configurations on selected models using tool- and code-based retrieval. The evaluation exposed category-specific failure modes and showed that performance can vary with the source IFC model and retrieval interface. IFC-MCQ enables scalable benchmarking of LLM-based IFC retrieval in AEC workflows.

top_articles.title: FusionEval: Benchmarking Model Fusion for Large Language Models
top_articles.title_original: FusionEval: Benchmarking Model Fusion for Large Language Models
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.30162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model fusion aims to integrate the capabilities of multi-expert models into a single model. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage of reasoning with long chains of thought and tool use, while strong average performance can mask substantial losses in individual expert capabilities. We introduce FusionEval, a benchmark that provides controlled expert pools, integrates fusion methods with and without additional training, and offers a unified evaluation suite. The pools contain domain experts independently trained from Qwen3 and Llama base models across math, code, science, instruction following, and tool use. The suite evaluates capability retention and computational cost on eight public benchmarks under comparable data access rules, reporting normalized average and worst performance, runtime, and peak GPU memory usage. Extensive experiments show that training-free methods preserve reasoning performance but substantially degrade tool use at both model scales. In contrast, MOPD preserves tool use and achieves a more balanced capability profile, but requires additional data preparation, inference, and training. Jointly retaining reasoning, instruction following, and tool use at low computational cost remains a challenge. We hope FusionEval supports future research on efficient model fusion that jointly preserves expert capabilities. Our code is available at https://github.com/Baicaihaochi/FusionEval_Benchmark.

top_articles.title: SWE-VERIFIER: Selective Verification for Cost-Efficient Coding Agents
top_articles.title_original: SWE-VERIFIER: Selective Verification for Cost-Efficient Coding Agents
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.30284v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents spend substantial computation generating actions and processing long interaction histories. Poor action choices can steer agents into low-value states, wasting computation and increasing API costs. Sampling and verifying alternative actions can improve the agent's decisions, but applying this procedure at every step adds substantial overhead. We introduce SWE-Verifier, a lightweight generative model that selectively triggers candidate sampling and verification. It scores the coding agent's proposed action to determine when additional candidate sampling is needed, then ranks the resulting actions before execution. We train SWE-Verifier from Qwen3.5-4B using preference data that groups contrasting actions with their resulting environment observations and rubric-guided teacher scores. Using the mini-swe-agent harness, SWE-Verifier improves resolution from 75.47% to 77.20% on MiniMax-M2.7 at 1.09 times cost and generalizes to DeepSeek-V4-Flash without training on its actions, improving resolution from 72.60% to 74.27% at 1.13 times cost. Across both models, SWE-Verifier verifies fewer than 4% of steps and achieves comparable or higher resolution than the trajectory and all-step baselines at substantially lower cost. These results demonstrate that selective candidate sampling and lightweight verification provide complementary gains in coding-agent performance and inference efficiency. Our model, code, and data are available at https://github.com/zkjzou/SWE-Verifier.

top_articles.title: Exploration via Activation-Space Steering for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
top_articles.title_original: Exploration via Activation-Space Steering for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.27012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains a language model by sampling responses, scoring them with an automatic verifier, and updating the policy from the resulting rewards. The policy therefore receives direct learning signals only from trajectories that appear in its rollouts. Yet repeated sampling from the same policy can concentrate on similar reasoning paths, leaving useful alternatives unexplored under a fixed rollout budget. We introduce Activation-Space Exploration (ASE), an online method for diversifying training rollouts. By clustering activation differences between correct and incorrect responses to the same problem, ASE builds a structured bank of latent exploration vectors. Different vectors are then applied to subsequent rollouts to explore alternative reasoning paths. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base trained on DAPO-Math-17k, ASE improves average Mean@8 across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks over GRPO by 4.87 and 1.87 percentage points, respectively, under the same rollout budget.

top_articles.title: MoEZip: Routing-Aware KV Cache Compression for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
top_articles.title_original: MoEZip: Routing-Aware KV Cache Compression for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.30206v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models scale model capacity efficiently by activating a small subset of parameters per token. However, in long-context inference, memory remains a major bottleneck because the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length. Existing KV cache compression methods reduce this cost for dense transformers, but overlook a problem specific to MoE: KV eviction can change which experts are selected during answer generation, degrading the generation quality. We propose MoEZip, a routing-aware KV cache compression for sparse MoE language models. To estimate the sensitivity of expert routing to perturbation, we propose a novel metric based on the Fisher information matrix of routing distributions. MoEZip combines this metric with attention weights for routing-aware scoring of contexts. Finally, we compose a complementary scoring system that combines eviction methods for dense and sparse-MoE architectures. Experiments show that MoEZip achieves robust performance under aggressive cache compression on various benchmarks. At a KV retention ratio of 10\%, MoEZip improves over the SoTA baseline by +24 and +20 points on average on LongBench and RULER, corresponding to 2.3$\times$ and 4.9$\times$ higher scores, respectively.

top_articles.title_original: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
top_articles.summary: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied : Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do. As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that: Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. top_articles.summary: IT之家 10 月 24 日消息，据中国信通院，随着大模型技术的迅速迭代，词元（Token）服务成为从技术走向应用的关键点，我国日均词元调用量持续攀升，2026 年 6 月， 国内词元日均消耗量约 500 万亿 ，是 2025 年 12 月的近 4 倍。产业中越来越多的 MaaS（Model as a Service，模型即服务）平台厂商通过公有云 API 方式供给大模型词元服务。然而用户对词元服务性能缺乏直观的判断依据，且面临选型困难等各类问题。 为有效衡量服务性能，中国信息通信研究院（简称“中国信通院”）人工智能研究所、人工智能大模型及软硬件评测工业和信息化部重点实验室和中国人工智能产业发展联盟，自 2025 年以来持续开展公有云大模型词元服务性能监测工作，为产业应用提供重要参考，现联合发布《大模型词元服务性能监测报告（2026 年）》。 报告基于 2026 年 1-8 月的监测数据，围绕各平台词元服务调用成功率、吞吐速度、首词时延、稳定性、价格、上下文窗口等维度开展分析，对比原厂大模型官方平台，以及 DeepSeek、Qwen、GLM、Kimi 四款开源模型在第三方平台上的性能差异，进一步分析影响词元服务性能的关键因素，总结产业核心观察，明确下一步工作计划，旨在为用户选型提供参考，并为产业界优化服务能力提供方向指引。 IT之家附报告核心观点： 1. 国内词元服务每秒吞吐量较 2025 年翻倍，仍低于国外 报告提出，8 月份国内各模型平均 TPS（每秒输出词元数）达到 78.23（个 / 秒），与 2025 年均值 38.25（个 / 秒）相比实现翻倍。但 8 月份国外典型模型的 TPS 均值为 112.82（个 / 秒），与 2025 年 12 月的 51.35（个 / 秒）相比，提升亦超过一倍，整体优于国内。 ▲ 所有大模型词元服务月均 TPS 2. 词元服务时延有所增加，国内外趋势一致 报告提出，今年以来，国内各模型的平均 TTFT（首词时延）呈现持续提升态势，8 月份均值达到 1.26 秒，相较于 2025 年平均值 0.78 秒明显增加。但同时 8 月份国外典型模型 TTFT 平均值达到 2.08 秒，相比 4 月份 1.04 秒亦明显增加。值得注意的是，TTFT 上升并非单纯的性能退化，而是伴随着模型参数量增加、上下文长度增加、调用量增加等多种因素同步产生的结果。 ▲ 所有大模型词元服务的月均 TTFT 3. 2026 年词元服务价格明显回升 报告提出，经历了过去两年价格战后，2026 年国内外模型服务价格明显上涨。国内 2025 下半年归一化均价为 6.8 元，而今年以来均价为 13.46 元，涨幅接近 1 倍。但国外价格仍高于国内，2026 年以来发布的典型模型平均归一价格约为 117.8 元。 ▲ 国内原厂大模型发布时归一化价格趋势图 4. 模型上下文长度不断向百万级长度扩展 报告提出，被监测的模型中，上下文长度达到 1M（1 百万词元）的模型占比 47.8%，200K 及以上的合计达 95.7%，相比 2025 年底的占比提高超过 76 个百分点，而低于 200K 的模型占比持续减少。 ▲ 国内原厂大模型发布时归一化价格趋势图 5. 开源模型词元服务性能提升显著，同一模型在不同平台性能波动较大 报告提出，5 月份更新了 4 款开源模型的新版本进行监测，结果显示 TPS 持续提升，TTFT 时延不断压缩。例如 8 月份 DeepSeek-V4-Pro 的 TPS 已达到 DeepSeek-V3.2 的 2 倍。时延方面，5 月份主要模型完成换代升级后，TTFT 普遍出现阶段性上升，随着推理优化措施落地，时延指标逐步回落至换代前水平。同时，4 款模型在不同平台上的 TPS、TTFT、调用成功率表现不一。部分第三方平台性能明显优于官方平台提供的模型服务，同一模型在不同平台间的 TPS 差距最大可接近一倍。各平台对相同模型的推理加速、优化策略、成本控制不同，是造成性能分化的主要原因。 ▲ 开源模型性能综合对比图

top_articles.title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?
top_articles.title_original: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.28763v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (https://github.com/maszhongming/agent4sci) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MingZhong/agent4sci).

top_articles.title: StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and Training Autonomous Operator Agents
top_articles.title_original: StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and Training Autonomous Operator Agents
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.10942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning environments are now a primary lever for improving large language model (LLM) capabilities in post-training, yet most agentic benchmarks remain static: the world moves only when the agent acts, the reward is a terminal verdict, and the pass bar is set arbitrarily. We introduce StoreBench, a live-commerce environment in which an agent runs a mid-size online apparel store on a production-grade commerce backend, testing long-horizon planning and economic judgment under uncertainty. Customers order around the clock, suppliers reprice and fail, and market shocks arrive with partial or no warning. The agent acts through the same 29 merchant tools a human operator would use, under a windowed operation budget that makes simulated time a function of actions taken, so model latency cannot influence simulated time. Pass thresholds are calibrated against scripted anchor policies, the reward is hardened against a catalogue of reward hacks, and every episode replays identically given a sequence of actions. We evaluate seven frontier LLMs on 11 scenarios of 30 to 45 days and a full simulated year, over three world seeds at matched reasoning effort. No model matches the scripted smart-triage policy on average: the best, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, passes 49% of task-seed cells against the heuristic's 97%. Human experts working through the same tools and budgets outscore every model (mean composite 0.708 vs. 0.700). Over a full simulated year under the Claude Code harness, most models show dramatic performance improvement. In a GRPO post-training run, Qwen3.5-27B trained on only five disjoint tasks raises its mean composite on the held-out evaluation tasks from 0.136 to 0.373. We release five example training-split tasks, ten sample trajectories, and the scoring and verification tooling; the full environment and evaluation suite are withheld to keep the benchmark uncontaminated.

top_articles.title: Behavior Beyond Text: Evaluating Refusal Transfer Failure in LLM Agents
top_articles.title_original: Behavior Beyond Text: Evaluating Refusal Transfer Failure in LLM Agents
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.28982v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While large language models are increasingly deployed as tool-calling agents, their safety evaluations still focus primarily on their ability to refuse harmful requests in text. We investigate whether the refusal behavior in text transfers to tool use. We construct a benchmark of 2,304 prompts across four domains, consisting of matched triplets that present the same harmful or benign request in text-only, standard tool-enabled, and adversarially framed tool-enabled settings. We then assess tool-call safety using 20 predefined forbidden actions. Testing five models of varying sizes and families, we find that requests refused in text frequently result in unsafe tool calls. Under standard tool-enabled prompting, this divergence occurs for 10-52 percent of harmful requests refused in chat. To mechanistically investigate this gap, we identify a refusal-associated direction in the residual stream of each of the five models. We find that in tool-enabled contexts, the activations along this direction decrease in four of five models. Furthermore, lower activation predicts unsafe tool calls across all five models (AUC 0.76-0.86). However, restoring the signal to the respective text-only value through activation patching only prevents a subset of unsafe calls, primarily by suppressing tool use rather than by producing safer calls. Steering along the refusal direction nearly eliminates unsafe calls only at strengths that also suppress benign tool use or degrade the output quality. Our findings indicate that the identified refusal direction contributes to whether a model acts, but only partially explains the refusal divergence. Therefore, evaluating the safety of tool-calling agents requires directly examining their actions along with their textual responses.

top_articles.title: Spectral Smoothing and Spiking Perturbations Reconfigure Capability Profiles and Selective Task Performance in Large Language Models
top_articles.title_original: Spectral Smoothing and Spiking Perturbations Reconfigure Capability Profiles and Selective Task Performance in Large Language Models
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.30676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Singular-value spectra encode important structure in transformer feed-forward projections, yet their causal role in downstream behavior remains underexplored. We study post-hoc spectral smoothing and spiking interventions on the up_proj and down_proj matrices. Positive perturbation stretches deviations from the geometric mean, making large singular values larger and small ones smaller (spiking), and vice versa. The intervention preserves singular vectors and the geometric mean of the singular values. Across five open Llama and Qwen instruction models, we evaluate the perturbed systems on capability-labeled subtasks, standard and chain-of-thought reasoning benchmarks, judge-scored truthfulness, hallucination, and safety tasks, and TRAIT personality probes. To interpret score shifts, we fit responses in a three-dimensional capability basis consisting of factual knowledge, language understanding, and deductive reasoning. The induced changes suggest structured rather than purely random sensitivity: large positive perturbations more reliably suppress language and deductive responses, moderate negative perturbations can sometimes improve factual or task-local performance on the evaluated grids, and sensitivity varies strongly by model family, benchmark module, and underlying layerwise spectral inequality. These results position spectral perturbation as a lightweight intervention for probing how capabilities are organized and traded off in large language models.

top_articles.title: IFC-MCQ: Automatically Generating Multiple-Choice Benchmarks for Evaluating LLM Agents on IFC Data Retrieval
top_articles.title_original: IFC-MCQ: Automatically Generating Multiple-Choice Benchmarks for Evaluating LLM Agents on IFC Data Retrieval
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.30533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Industry Foundation Classes (IFC), the standard for building information exchange in architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC), is increasingly queried through large language models (LLMs) using natural language. Evaluating these systems at scale is difficult because free-text answers require costly human or LLM-based review. We propose IFC-MCQ, a method that automatically generates multiple-choice benchmarks from IFC files for exact option-set grading. The taxonomy covers 15 categories and 36 subtypes across four groups, with answer keys derived from the file and distractors constructed from file-derived values or predefined rules. We applied IFC-MCQ to IFC models of varying sizes and modelling characteristics to assess generation coverage and evaluated two agentic configurations on selected models using tool- and code-based retrieval. The evaluation exposed category-specific failure modes and showed that performance can vary with the source IFC model and retrieval interface. IFC-MCQ enables scalable benchmarking of LLM-based IFC retrieval in AEC workflows.

top_articles.title: FusionEval: Benchmarking Model Fusion for Large Language Models
top_articles.title_original: FusionEval: Benchmarking Model Fusion for Large Language Models
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.30162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model fusion aims to integrate the capabilities of multi-expert models into a single model. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage of reasoning with long chains of thought and tool use, while strong average performance can mask substantial losses in individual expert capabilities. We introduce FusionEval, a benchmark that provides controlled expert pools, integrates fusion methods with and without additional training, and offers a unified evaluation suite. The pools contain domain experts independently trained from Qwen3 and Llama base models across math, code, science, instruction following, and tool use. The suite evaluates capability retention and computational cost on eight public benchmarks under comparable data access rules, reporting normalized average and worst performance, runtime, and peak GPU memory usage. Extensive experiments show that training-free methods preserve reasoning performance but substantially degrade tool use at both model scales. In contrast, MOPD preserves tool use and achieves a more balanced capability profile, but requires additional data preparation, inference, and training. Jointly retaining reasoning, instruction following, and tool use at low computational cost remains a challenge. We hope FusionEval supports future research on efficient model fusion that jointly preserves expert capabilities. Our code is available at https://github.com/Baicaihaochi/FusionEval_Benchmark.

top_articles.title: SWE-VERIFIER: Selective Verification for Cost-Efficient Coding Agents
top_articles.title_original: SWE-VERIFIER: Selective Verification for Cost-Efficient Coding Agents
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.30284v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents spend substantial computation generating actions and processing long interaction histories. Poor action choices can steer agents into low-value states, wasting computation and increasing API costs. Sampling and verifying alternative actions can improve the agent's decisions, but applying this procedure at every step adds substantial overhead. We introduce SWE-Verifier, a lightweight generative model that selectively triggers candidate sampling and verification. It scores the coding agent's proposed action to determine when additional candidate sampling is needed, then ranks the resulting actions before execution. We train SWE-Verifier from Qwen3.5-4B using preference data that groups contrasting actions with their resulting environment observations and rubric-guided teacher scores. Using the mini-swe-agent harness, SWE-Verifier improves resolution from 75.47% to 77.20% on MiniMax-M2.7 at 1.09 times cost and generalizes to DeepSeek-V4-Flash without training on its actions, improving resolution from 72.60% to 74.27% at 1.13 times cost. Across both models, SWE-Verifier verifies fewer than 4% of steps and achieves comparable or higher resolution than the trajectory and all-step baselines at substantially lower cost. These results demonstrate that selective candidate sampling and lightweight verification provide complementary gains in coding-agent performance and inference efficiency. Our model, code, and data are available at https://github.com/zkjzou/SWE-Verifier.

top_articles.title: Exploration via Activation-Space Steering for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
top_articles.title_original: Exploration via Activation-Space Steering for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.27012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains a language model by sampling responses, scoring them with an automatic verifier, and updating the policy from the resulting rewards. The policy therefore receives direct learning signals only from trajectories that appear in its rollouts. Yet repeated sampling from the same policy can concentrate on similar reasoning paths, leaving useful alternatives unexplored under a fixed rollout budget. We introduce Activation-Space Exploration (ASE), an online method for diversifying training rollouts. By clustering activation differences between correct and incorrect responses to the same problem, ASE builds a structured bank of latent exploration vectors. Different vectors are then applied to subsequent rollouts to explore alternative reasoning paths. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base trained on DAPO-Math-17k, ASE improves average Mean@8 across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks over GRPO by 4.87 and 1.87 percentage points, respectively, under the same rollout budget.

top_articles.title: MoEZip: Routing-Aware KV Cache Compression for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
top_articles.title_original: MoEZip: Routing-Aware KV Cache Compression for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
top_articles.summary: arXiv:2610.30206v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models scale model capacity efficiently by activating a small subset of parameters per token. However, in long-context inference, memory remains a major bottleneck because the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length. Existing KV cache compression methods reduce this cost for dense transformers, but overlook a problem specific to MoE: KV eviction can change which experts are selected during answer generation, degrading the generation quality. We propose MoEZip, a routing-aware KV cache compression for sparse MoE language models. To estimate the sensitivity of expert routing to perturbation, we propose a novel metric based on the Fisher information matrix of routing distributions. MoEZip combines this metric with attention weights for routing-aware scoring of contexts. Finally, we compose a complementary scoring system that combines eviction methods for dense and sparse-MoE architectures. Experiments show that MoEZip achieves robust performance under aggressive cache compression on various benchmarks. At a KV retention ratio of 10\%, MoEZip improves over the SoTA baseline by +24 and +20 points on average on LongBench and RULER, corresponding to 2.3$\times$ and 4.9$\times$ higher scores, respectively.
